prompt: Why can the central firewall not enforce microsegmentation on its own?
hint: Which packets does it see?

choices.text: It has too few rules for two hundred machines
choices.why: The count of rules is not the obstacle.

choices.text: Traffic inside a segment does not cross it
choices.why: Right. Two machines on one switch talk past it.

choices.text: It filters by port, and microsegmentation needs roles
choices.why: The generated host rules filter by address and port too.

choices.text: Stateful firewalls cannot be placed between zones
choices.why: Lesson 4 put exactly that between the zones.

prompt: Match each property to its value under microsegmentation.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

pairs.right: each host, or the hypervisor next to it
closed unless a rule allows it

prompt: A team runs 300 containers and wants each one isolated from the rest. What keeps that from becoming 300 rule sets nobody can keep consistent?
hint: Where is the policy written, and how many times?

choices.text: A larger central firewall with one rule per container pair
choices.why: Traffic between containers on one host never reaches it.

choices.text: Putting the containers back into three zones
choices.why: That reopens everything inside each zone.

choices.text: One policy by role, with the platform generating each container's rules
choices.why: Right. The mechanism differs; the policy has the same shape.

choices.text: Writing each container's rules by hand, carefully
choices.why: Hand-written host firewalls drift apart at that scale.

prompt: A second application server is added to policy.txt with the role app. What does it need before it can reach the database?
hint: Where is a role turned into addresses?

choices.text: A new accept line typed into db's rules
choices.why: Nobody edits db's rules; they are generated.

choices.text: The rules generated again
choices.why: Right. Its address joins the role app at the next generation.

choices.text: A new row naming db in its from column
choices.why: The from column names roles that connect in, not the target.

choices.text: Its address added to db's row, next to app
choices.why: Addresses never appear in the from column.

prompt: After loading its generated rules, how many lines of db's input chain contain accept?
hint: grep -c accept counted them.

prompt: The from column names roles, and each role is turned into ___ only when the rules are generated.
hint: What does the generated rule put after ip saddr?

prompt: Why does each generated accept rule carry a comment such as "postgres from app"?
hint: Whose words are in it?

choices.text: nft refuses an accept rule without one
choices.why: A comment is optional in nft.

choices.text: The generator reads it back to find the role
choices.why: It reads policy.txt, not its own output.

choices.text: So the rule says why it exists, in the policy's words
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It records who generated the rule and when
choices.why: It holds the service and the roles, not an author.

prompt: Which of these connections is east-west?
hint: Between whom does it run?

choices.text: A browser at home reaching www
choices.why: Client to server is north-south.

choices.text: An employee's laptop reaching the proxy
choices.why: Still a client reaching a server.

choices.text: A DNS answer returning to a laptop
choices.why: A reply to a client, north-south.

choices.text: app connecting to db on 5432
choices.why: Right. Server to server.

prompt: Which probes came back open after the generated rules were loaded? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare each with the policy's rows.

choices.text: app to db:5432
choices.why: postgres from app.

choices.text: www to app:8080
choices.why: http from proxy, and www is the proxy.

choices.text: db to app:22
choices.why: SSH is from the admin role.

choices.text: admin to db:5432
choices.why: postgres is from app; admin gets SSH.

choices.text: admin to db:22
choices.why: ssh from admin, on every host.

prompt: An attacker takes over app. With the generated rules in place, what on the servers segment can app still reach?
hint: Read app's probe of db.

choices.text: Everything on its segment, since fw is not in the way
choices.why: That was before this lesson.

choices.text: db's SSH and the database, as its neighbour
choices.why: db:22 came back blocked.

choices.text: Port 5432 on db
choices.why: Right. The one port the application needs.

choices.text: No other machine at all
choices.why: db:5432 came back open.

prompt: An operator adds an accept rule on db by hand to fix an outage, and a week later the policy changes. What happens to the hand-made rule?
hint: How does every generated file start?

choices.text: It stays, because nft merges old rules into new ones
choices.why: The file starts with flush ruleset.

choices.text: The next generation removes it without a word
choices.why: Right. The fix belongs in the policy file.

choices.text: The generator refuses to run until it is removed
choices.why: The generator does not read the host's rules.

choices.text: It is copied into policy.txt automatically
choices.why: Nothing flows from a host back to the policy.

prompt: db's accept line for app on 5432 was removed while a session was open. Why did the client's second line still arrive?
hint: Which rule comes first on every host?

choices.text: nft -f takes a minute to apply
choices.why: The count of 5432 rules was already 0.

choices.text: The admin role still had access to db
choices.why: admin reaches SSH, and the client was app.

choices.text: ct state established accepted it, as the session predated the change
choices.why: Right. The new policy governs new connections.

choices.text: The line travelled over UDP, which the rule did not cover
choices.why: It was a TCP session on 5432.

prompt: How many seconds after its first line did app send the second one?
hint: The section says it.

prompt: An employee is removed from the VPN's allowed group at noon while connected. With only the rule changed, when does their access end?
hint: What did db do with the session that was already open?

choices.text: At noon, when the rule changes
choices.why: The rule decides new connections, not open ones.

choices.text: When that session ends and they try to connect again
choices.why: Right. Until then, nothing re-verifies it.

choices.text: At the next packet they send after noon
choices.why: The second line on db went through after the change.

choices.text: After the TIME_WAIT of the change expires
choices.why: TIME_WAIT belongs to a closed connection, not to a rule.

prompt: How many conntrack flow entries did the withdrawal delete on db?
hint: The message after conntrack -D.

prompt: Only one session was open, yet conntrack deleted two entries. What was the other?
hint: Think of the earlier run.

choices.text: The reply direction of the same session
choices.why: One entry holds both directions.

choices.text: admin's SSH session to db
choices.why: The deletion matched port 5432 from app.

choices.text: A UDP flow on 5432
choices.why: -p tcp matched TCP entries.

choices.text: The previous session, closed and waiting out TIME_WAIT
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Match each layer to how a live session is ended there.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.right: clear its session table for the address
invalidate the session on the server side
revoke the tokens and keep lifetimes short

prompt: A company revokes a contractor's SSO account, and nothing ends the sessions already open. Which setting decides when their access really stops?
hint: A revocation that leaves sessions running is a schedule. Of what?

choices.text: The tokens' lifetime
choices.why: Right. It takes effect within one lifetime.

choices.text: The password policy's minimum length
choices.why: A password is checked at sign-in, which is over.

choices.text: The firewall's conntrack timeout for established TCP
choices.why: That is a host firewall's clock, not the SSO grant's.

choices.text: How often the account directory is backed up
choices.why: A backup does not re-verify anybody.

prompt: Order the steps that withdraw app from the database completely, from first to last.
hint: Policy first, open sessions last.
items: remove app from the from roles of db's row in policy.txt
load the new rules on db with nft -f
delete app's conntrack entries for port 5432
trap: Deleting the entries before the new rules are loaded lets the next packet open a new session under the old rule.

prompt: A new reporting server, role report, must read the database. What is the reviewed change?
hint: Where does a change of who may reach the database live?

choices.text: An accept line for its address, typed on db and reloaded
choices.why: The next generation would flush it.

choices.text: A row for the host, and report added to db's from roles
choices.why: Right. A diff to policy.txt, then generation.

choices.text: A rule on fw between its segment and the servers
choices.why: db's own rules would still drop it.

choices.text: The role app for the new server
choices.why: It would then also be accepted wherever app is.

prompt: After a change to the policy, which check shows the east-west matrix is really what the table says?
hint: Where was each cell tested from?

choices.text: Reading the generated files for the right accept lines
choices.why: That checks the file, not what is loaded and reachable.

choices.text: Probing each server from fw
choices.why: East-west traffic never crosses fw.

choices.text: Counting accept lines on each host
choices.why: Four lines can still be the wrong four.

choices.text: Probing every cell from its own source machine
choices.why: Right. That is how the section tested it.
